clinicalPearls: One of the commonest sports injuries, typically occurring during high-speed running or sudden stretching of the posterior thigh
Patients describe a sudden sharp posterior thigh pain, sometimes with a pop, and difficulty continuing activity
The biceps femoris is the most frequently injured of the hamstring muscles in sprinting-type injuries
Injuries are graded by severity, and proximal free tendon or bony avulsion injuries behave differently and may need surgery
A large proximal avulsion, especially with retraction, warrants prompt orthopaedic assessment
Recurrence is common, so structured rehabilitation and graded return to sport are important
reference.pathophysiology: Hamstring strain occurs when tensile load on the muscle-tendon unit exceeds its capacity, usually during the late swing phase of sprinting when the hamstrings contract eccentrically while lengthening. This generates high forces that tear muscle fibres, most often at the musculotendinous junction of the biceps femoris. Stretch-type injuries from combined hip flexion and knee extension tend to involve the proximal free tendon. Incomplete rehabilitation, reduced eccentric strength and scar tissue predispose to the high recurrence rate.
additionalDifferentials: Referred pain from the lumbar spine or sciatic nerve
Adductor or other thigh muscle strain
Deep vein thrombosis (for posterior leg pain and swelling)
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment of site, strength and the mechanism of injury
Ultrasound or MRI to grade injury and identify tendon or avulsion involvement
Assessment for proximal avulsion requiring surgical referral
Evaluation of the lumbar spine if referral is suspected
Functional testing to guide return to sport
redFlags: Adolescent with suspected ischial apophyseal avulsion
Posterior leg swelling raising concern for venous thrombosis
reference.prognosis: Most muscular strains recover with graded rehabilitation, but recovery time varies with grade and site, and recurrence is frequent; proximal avulsions may require surgery for best outcomes.
pitfalls: Missing a proximal tendon avulsion that benefits from early surgery
Returning to sport before adequate eccentric strength is restored
Overlooking an adolescent ischial apophyseal avulsion
Attributing posterior thigh pain to a strain when it is referred from the spine
